title: Vellum Venom: 2026 Audi RS e-tron GT

body_markdown:
Looksmaxxing is a modern beauty trend that’s generously defined as looking your best on social media. The lengths people go to enhance their look to the max[can be unsafe](https://www.michiganmedicine.org/health-lab/what-looksmaxxing#:~:text=Bravender%3A%E2%80%AFParents%20need%20to%20be%20aware%20of%20these%20behaviors%20and%20confront%20them%20straight%20on%20if%20they%20see%20signs%20their%20kids%20are%20trying%20them.) , but when it comes to cars, the trend is a little more palatable. Once in a while you see a car and know it’s been looksmaxxed *to the max.* One example that always looks like it’s flexing for the camera is the Audi RS e-tron GT, with steamroller-worthy wheels, fender flares, and a low-slung four-door cabin that take Audi’s current design DNA to a radical extreme.


But I didn’t necessarily feel that way until I took this particular Audi RS e-tron GT to a local car meet, and had the pleasure of parking beside a late-model Audi S4 sedan. It’s clear which Audi is looksmaxxing for the social media cred, and who is just out here living their best life.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


Audi


Audi


It’s okay for car brands to looksmaxx (as it were) because there’s no significant downside to their health in such aggressive styling. You could also argue that the original Audi GT coupe was expertly looksmaxxed with the Sport Quattro’s shorter wheelbase and box-flare fenders. But the Audi RS e-tron GT isn’t derived from another product bearing Audi’s famous Four Rings logo; instead, it’s another take on the ground-hugging stance of Porsche’s Taycan EV. Here, we’ll unpack that effort and seek to understand from a design perspective whether or not that was a good idea.


We covered the Taycan[back in 2020](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-2020-porsche-taycan-turbo-s/) , so let’s take this $192,000 Audi for a run on the vellum to see if the style is worthy of the muscular, 900+ horsepower performance underneath the skin.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


The approach is strong, but it darn well better be for a $192,000 price tag. Base models start at $170,500, and they all look the same from this angle: There’s a long and prestigious hood (by new-car standards), squinty headlights with serious detailing inside, and angry triangular forms.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


The 2004 A6 started a phenomenon.


Audi


My goodness, we have come a long way since 2004.


The[gaping maw](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-a-glossary-of-automotive-design-terms/#:~:text=Gaping%20Maw%3A%20oversized%20grilles%20and%20cooling%20ducts%20that%20dominate%20a%20front%20fascia.%20Generally%20used%20as%20a%20pejorative%2C%20as%20it%20allows%20for%20the%20addition%20of%20non%2Dfunctional%20blackout%20panels%20popularized%20by%20the%202004%20Audi%20A4%20and%20A6.) school of design that once made a new Audi sedan look like the stunning[Rosemeyer concept](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audi_Rosemeyer) has now turned into masses of grayscale plastic, bathroom-grade geometric texturing, and a handy spot to tuck away some sensors for driver’s assists. While I am no fan of the original gaping maw A6, I do long for the day when “heavy” chrome accenting and logical linear patterns signified a luxury/premium vehicle.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


Audi


Not to get too nostalgic for the aforementioned A6, but the prevailing school of taut, tense creases in the fender and the hood areas is getting a bit overdone. That critique isn’t unique to Audi’s e-tron GT, but it would be nice to see clean, uncluttered surfaces on a flagship Audi in the near futu… *wait, my[prayers have been answered!](https://www.hagerty.com/media/design/audis-nuvolari-is-back-and-this-time-its-no-concept/)*


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


Bodies are just too busy these days, but it’s nice to see how Audi made their “four rings” corporate emblem integrate into the front bumper. The round elements are a nice balance to all the angry bends and stretched-out hexagons we see elsewhere on the front end.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


These laser-equipped headlights are architecturally stunning. Spend some time staring, and you feel like you’re looking down on a miniature sci-fi set for a movie like *The Running Man* , *Robocop* , or *Total Recall* . Only the amber reflector at the corner looks mundane!


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


The hood-to-fender and fender-to-front fascia cut lines are disjointed next to those stunning laser lights. That’s unfortunate, as the front bumper and headlight contouring play very nicely in the same sandbox. The e-tron GT is already a busy looking car, and those cut lines do it no favors.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


This mix of gloss and matte black does a good job integrating cooling and safety features. The hexagons in the grille also become a recurring theme elsewhere on the body. The problems surface when you step back and try to integrate these into the rest of the front fascia.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


The contrast between solid and open hexagons is a daring choice, as one texture can negate the other. The solid hexagons are somewhat useless by nature, and it takes away from the hard work performed by the open ones. There’s plenty to process with that, and then consider how round rings and hexagon textures might be unpleasant to some eyes.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


Audi


But there’s a balance between solid and hollow, round and angular. My concern is how the gloss black bumper trim wraps up and over the gray hexagonal grille. The effect doesn’t feel prestigious or elegant to my eyes, as the[body-color bumper integration](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-2021-kia-soul/#:~:text=Next-,Sajeev%20Mehta,-It%E2%80%99s%20probably%20a) of something like the Kia Soul makes more sense if you are old enough to equate black plastic with cheap cars. This particular example got off lucky, because the gray hood/grille doesn’t stand out too much, at least compared to examples finished in white.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


It’s unfortunate that Audi avoided adding a flashy-looking[front splitter](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-a-glossary-of-automotive-design-terms/#:~:text=Splitter%3A%20A%20front%20valance%20that%20splits%20air%20and%20pushes%20the%20higher%20pressure%20air%20over%20the%20car%20to%20increase%20downforce%20at%20speed.) to the bottom of the e-tron’s front bumper. Doing so helps justify the need to paint the center of the front fascia that glossy black finish. A little more forward thrust would give a unique landscape for the color, as putting everything on the same plane is a bit dull.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


More forward thrust would also help the bumper from this angle, as it’s otherwise a tall affair lacking in depth. While it’s far from bland or subtle, this fascia is severely underselling the performance underneath. Porsche’s counterpart (the Taycan) has more depth in this area, but this Audi has a more urgent need for swagger since it lacks an emblem with the word “Stuttgart” in it.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


The muscular hood and fender creases here create visual interest, but they are too subtle for what’s underneath. While it’s disingenuous to suggest this Audi’s aggressive creases lack the impression of high-performance machinery, its sports car proportioning (long, low, and taut) presents a unique opportunity to elevate the styling in a manner no other brand could accomplish.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


These creases suggest a lack of brand awareness, a theme that continues down the body. With 900 horsepower matched with flawless dynamics, the e-tron deserves a more Audi Sport Quattro,[box-flare](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-a-glossary-of-automotive-design-terms/#:~:text=Box%20Flare%3A%20Flared%20fender%20contouring%20reminiscent%20of%20a%20box%2C%20popularized%20by%20Group%20B%20rally%20cars%20and%20highly%20associated%20with%20the%201985%20Audi%20Sport%20Quattro.) demeanor in its body-side styling. Instead, we get a fender with a charging door and[air curtain](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-a-glossary-of-automotive-design-terms/#:~:text=Air%20curtains%3A%20Aerodynamic%20trick%20to%20reduce%20drag%20by%20directing%20air%20around%20the%20front%20wheels%2C%20often%20providing%20a%20marginal%20benefit%20to%20fuel%20economy.) that’s highly influenced by the Porsche Taycan.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


I am not suggesting that the Taycan’s three- to four-times higher sales volumes are because of this fender, but Audi could have really amped up the enthusiast base via box flares with integrated charging ports. Audi has a depth of sporting history and aggressive looks it could draw from without crossing over to excessively retro, and the fenders of this low-slung e-tron are arguably the biggest missed opportunity.


There are no such compromises with the wheels, as they are aggressive enough to feel right for an RS-grade Audi EV product.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


Perhaps I am being too harsh in my “more box flare” assessment, because the fenders are heavily flared to accommodate such a massive wheel and tire package. But this air curtain at the edge feels more afterthought than integrated design concept, and that makes me think a box flare would do an even better job integrating the functional needs of this car while adding even more Quattro-branded DNA into the package.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


The cowl is sunken deep below the fenders, but that feature isn’t necessarily appealing. Those inflated fenders climb up the A-pillar in a fashion that looks more like Audi was meeting a fixed hard point of the chassis than designing a particular look. This is something you see frequently on affordable cars that share platforms, not flagship sedans. Fit and finish wasn’t a problem, but you really have to mind this gap when examining it up close.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


The Taycan’s fender-to-A-pillar integration is light-years ahead, but the rest of the roof works well considering the car’s mission. That crease in the A-pillar wasn’t there in the Taycan I ran over the vellum, and this example’s carbon fiber roof is both aggressive-looking and eliminates the massive glass panel that makes the summer months almost unbearable inside.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


The black skull caps add a dash of aggressive uniqueness to an otherwise forgettable side view mirror, and Audi’s been accentuating the mirrors on its performance products for decades now. There’s nothing wrong with that, much like the welcomed familiarity of a conventional door handle that doesn’t need an electronic solenoid to do a party trick every time you approach the vehicle.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


While I take issue with the B-pillar’s ornamentation, that’s a discussion for the end of this article. The B-pillar flows nicely with the visual speed of the other two roof pillars, and the door cutline’s off-center location almost makes sense in a vehicle this aggressive-looking.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


The same thing may not apply to the off-center cuts used to make the rear door openings in the C-pillar, but pushing the painted surface’s cut line beyond that of the daylight opening does make the car look “faster” and less static.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


Except there’s a missed opportunity here, because pushing the rear door’s cut line back to that of the glass gives more room for designers to experiment with box flares. There’s a Taycan-like softness in the Audi’s C-pillar, and it isn’t feasible to change this element. But the rear quarter panels, conversely, are dying for a change from that rounded/organic break in the surface to something worthy of Audi’s Group B motorsport legacy.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


While the contouring of both the fender and the rear door is elegant and assertive, this thing was dying for the design equivalent of gluing boxes to the fenders and fiberglassing them in. It’s just too much like the organic style of the Porsche Taycan.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


The soft fenders have another unintended negative consequence: a contrived series of round curves fighting against hard, angular cut lines in the trunk. Box flares, due to their (ahem) boxy nature, would make those necessary cut lines in the trunk more understandable. Given the “UR” Sport Quattro’s shorter wheelbase/stubbier proportioning than its 1985 Audi Coupe GT counterpart, the beauty of that box-flared icon would easily translate onto this low-slung sedan with modest overhangs and prodigious power.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


I can see the box flares from here, as they’d start at the taillight corners and extend deep into the rear door. The flares should taper inward to the rear bumper at the same rate as the decklid sliding down to the taillight, and the mechanized spoiler can be deleted for a similarly boxy fixed example.


The spoiler can be subtle like that of the 1985 Coupe GT, but I recommend something as insane as the E30 BMW M3. Not because I necessarily care for flashy designs, but because the e-tron’s rearward visibility is already horrendous, and this absolute monster deserves far more aggressive styling.


Yes, a fixed wing is painfully trite in modern car design, and it’d defeat the point of active aerodynamics and EV range maximization. But the end result would be cheaper, cleaner-looking, and far more exciting.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


But the fly in the e-tron’s ointment isn’t necessarily a lack of retro touches; it’s the[DLO fail](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-a-glossary-of-automotive-design-terms/#:~:text=DLO%20FAIL%3A%20A%20lament%20for%20the%20proliferation%20of%20opaque%20plastic%20panels%20in%20lieu%20of%20glass%2C%20visually%20cheating%20the%20shape%20of%20a%20vehicle%E2%80%99s%20greenhouse.%20More%20info%20here.) in the deck lid. Safety glass can’t bend with the desired cut line, but both Audi and Porsche wanted to extend the rear glass to the rear spoiler. This feels like a misguided attempt to lure Tesla buyers (who are used to the long glass of the iconic Model S hatchback) into a more premium electric four-door. It looks worse on the E-tron’s busy trunk, at least compared to the uncluttered contours of the Taycan.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


There is just way too much going on here. Every non-glass panel should instead be finished in body color, and a fixed-wing homage to the Sport Quattro would eliminate confusing cut lines while throwing a genuine bone to brand loyalists.


Cars this expensive aren’t sold on hard facts; designs that tug on the heartstrings push folks into one brand over another. The Taycan always outsells the E-Tron GT, and Audi hasn’t provided enough clear visual identity to justify more EV foot traffic in their showrooms.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


I’ve made jokes about trunk openings worthy of a mail slot in the past, but the E-tron (and the Taycan) take the cake. Making this car a proper hatchback may hurt dynamic performance, but this asphalt-inhaling animal has plenty of performance to spare. And several sources (including the biased nature of dealership sales staff) suggest the hatchback design of the Taycan Cross Turismo makes it more valuable on the used car market than a regular Taycan sedan.


Hatchbacks are fine and dandy, as proven by the success of Tesla’s Model S. But this is an Audi Quattro, and the original Sport Quattro had a tiny decklid: it wouldn’t take much to harken back to that era and make the e-tron GT into something of a German Dodge Challenger with a cult-like following.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


This stunted trunk is too short to be this curvaceous. There’s also a furrowed brow above its taillights, getting visually thicker and droopier in the center. Maybe the thicker center section was needed to ensure Audi’s four rings emblem was prominently displayed in the rear. Fair enough, but the thin-thick nature of the red taillight doesn’t help elongate the short bottom. Better to undo all this aggressive surfacing complexity for something more deeply rooted in Audi’s motorsport heritage.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


The effort present within these taillights, however, is admirable. They possess the same architectural aggressiveness as the laser-equipped headlights, and have an exciting amount of depth. This was all the surfacing and contouring needed, because the rest of the deck lid should have remained blocky, aggressive, and downright unfinished.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


The rear bumper has that blocky aesthetic in spades, and it’s simply drowning in the excesses presented above the taillight. Even the RS logo’s font is crisp and understated, even if the freestanding parallelogram feels naked without half of the “R” inside its red area.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


Those sour feelings further curdle when looking at the RS graphics applied to the seats, the puddle lights, and the aforementioned B-pillar. Having the “R” outside the parallelogram feels almost like a cheap knockoff of an Audi RS, like buying a fake Birkin. The puddle light’s geometric branding has a lack of gravitas, while the B-pillar’s font feels almost Temu-grade.


But don’t take my word for it, peep the[RS seat font of a 2024 model](https://media.carsandbids.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=2080,quality=80/460ceb3ec26cef4b9eba8146c237867b255e29b4/photos/interior/rjj54Qjo-wgtqvUI.jpg?t=176824365854) and tell me which version suits an Audi better.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


Back to the rear bumper, as the gloss black bits below are angular, angry, and assertive, much like the front bumper. But unlike the front, there’s an impressive amount of depth to each element. It’s also heavily surfaced with bevels that give hard reflections, in stark contrast to the fussy nature of the deck lid.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


The center includes a lamp and the hexagon impressions found in the front end. It’s a bit over the top, but that works for a vehicle with mind-altering amounts of acceleration and grip.


Audi


Netcarshow | Audi


As Gucci Mane once said, “You get the bag and fumble it.” The Audi RS e-tron GT could have been so much more than an angry Porsche Taycan with a furrowed brow on its backside.


Success is far from guaranteed in our current EV adoption climate, but this animal could have been a brand-honest beast with charging doors integrated into box flares, with a functional slot opening like a[C6 Corvette door handle](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/the-c6-corvette-is-on-the-brink-of-becoming-a-collector-car/#image-4) mounted above that air curtain. And those rear tires are absolutely begging for Sport Quattro box flares and a fixed wing on a flat deck.


Looking back doesn’t necessarily move you forward, but this powerhouse deserved styling more true to its roots. Porsche DNA casts a long shadow these days, and more differentiation from the Taycan would be greatly appreciated.


Thank you for reading, I hope you have a wonderful day.


The post[Vellum Venom: 2026 Audi RS e-tron GT](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-2026-audi-rs-e-tron-gt/) appeared first on[Hagerty Media](https://www.hagerty.com/media) .
